newsitem.title: USA: U.S. airlines to see flat-to-lower Q2 results.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airlines to see flat-to-lower Q2 results.

text.p: Second quarter profits at several U.S. airlines will fall below last year's record levels, after the federal excise tax and fare wars cut into industry profits, analysts said.

Profits at four of the seven largest U.S. airlines will be lower than last year, analysts said, with Trans World Airlines Inc expected to post a loss. Only UAL Corp and US Airways Group Inc are likely to show measurable year-over-year gains, they said.

"It will be a pretty mediocre quarter when you look at year-to-year comparisons. But if you look at absolute earnings, there are still some near-record results and there's a level of sustained profitability that this industry hasn't seen in a long time," said Jeff Long, an airline analyst with J.P. Morgan.

Investors were rattled over the past month as analysts began to trim their second quarter earnings estimates, a shift from the first quarter when most airlines topped Wall Street expectations. Fears of tax proposals being mulled by Congress also put pressure on airline stocks.
"All of the estimates were being talked down instead of talked up. Investors are seeing some down earnings for the first time in a while," Long said.

The 10 major carriers are expected to post a total net profit of $1.5 billion in the second quarter, up five percent from $1.4 billion a year ago, said NatWest Securities' airline analyst Susan Donofrio.
The modest gains expected in the second quarter are in "stark contrast" to the 445 percent year-over-year earnings growth seen in the first quarter of 1997, Donofrio said.

During the second quarter ending June 30, airlines launched deep fare sales, putting too much inventory on sale at too low a price. Airlines generated traffic at the expense of revenue yield, said CS First Boston analyst Tom Schreier.
"There were a couple of sales that weren't structured particularly well," Schreier said.
The return of the 10-percent passenger-excise tax also ate away at revenues and profits, analyst said.
The passenger excise tax was not in place during last year's second quarter, which gave the industry a windfall of funds that normally go to the Federal Aviation Administration.

When the tax returned in March, airlines missed out on that extra money, making year-over-year revenue comparisons Although industry fundamentals remain strong, some analyst caution that airline earnings have hit peak levels.
"Based on what we know, we're seeing the best of them (earnings)," said Helane Becker, an analyst with Smith Barney.
Other analysts said the second quarter would be the most challenging of the year, with the third and the fourth quarters showing improvements due to strong travel demand and declining fuel prices.
